title: How accurately do symptom checker apps assign urgency? A narrative review for a regional health authority
subtitle: Vignette and real-patient evidence for a listing decision
statement: Two symptom checker apps have asked to be listed on the health authority's patient website. The digital health committee needs a readable account of how accurately such apps assign urgency levels, distinguishing vignette studies from studies with real patients, noting groups for whom accuracy may be worse, and listing what the companies should be asked to show before any listing.
whoAffected: People using the authority's website to decide where to seek care, emergency departments and telephone advice lines, and the committee that endorses tools.
whatHurts: Under-triage can delay care for serious illness; over-triage adds to crowded emergency departments; an endorsed app that performs worse for older people, children or people with limited English would widen inequities.
currentPractice: The authority lists no symptom checker; committee members have no summary of the evidence.
whyNow: Two listing requests are pending and the committee meets on 2027-02-22.
constraints: About 80 hours of my time and 12 hours of librarian time. Report due to the committee by 2027-02-15, readable by lay members. No contact with the two companies during the review.
patientCenteredGoal: People who use an endorsed tool are directed to the right level of care, and no group is directed less safely than others.
summary: Problem framed as a narrative review for a lay committee deciding on app listing.
